{{distinguish|Spherical mean (statistics)}}
[[File:Spherical mean.png|right|thumb|The spherical mean of a function <math>u</math> (shown in red) is the average of the values <math>u(y)</math> (top, in blue) with <math>y</math> on a "sphere" of given radius around a given point (bottom, in blue).]]
In [[mathematics]], the '''spherical mean''' of a [[function (mathematics)|function]] around a point is the average of all values of that function on a sphere of given radius centered at that point.

==Definition==
Consider an [[open set]] ''U'' in the [[Euclidean space]] '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> and a [[continuous function]] ''u'' defined on ''U'' with [[real number|real]] or [[complex number|complex]] values. Let ''x'' be a point in ''U'' and ''r''&nbsp;&gt;&nbsp;0 be such that the [[closed set|closed]] [[ball (mathematics)|ball]] ''B''(''x'',&nbsp;''r'') of center ''x'' and radius ''r'' is contained in ''U''.  The '''spherical mean''' over the sphere of radius ''r'' centered at ''x'' is defined as

: <math>\frac{1}{\omega_{n-1}(r)}\int\limits_{\partial B(x, r)} \! u(y) \, \mathrm{d} S(y) </math>

where &part;''B''(''x'',&nbsp;''r'') is the [[n-sphere|(''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1)-sphere]] forming the [[boundary (topology)|boundary]] of ''B''(''x'',&nbsp;''r''), d''S'' denotes integration with respect to [[spherical measure]] and ''&omega;''<sub>''n''&minus;1</sub>(''r'') is the "surface area" of this (''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1)-sphere.

Equivalently, the spherical mean is given by

: <math>\frac{1}{\omega_{n-1}}\int\limits_{\|y\|=1} \! u(x+ry) \, \mathrm{d}S(y) </math>

where ''&omega;''<sub>''n''&minus;1</sub> is the area of the (''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1)-sphere of radius 1.

The spherical mean is often denoted as

: <math>\int\limits_{\partial B(x, r)}\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!-\,  u(y) \, \mathrm{d} S(y). </math>

The spherical mean is also defined for Riemannian manifolds in a natural manner.

==Properties and uses==

* From the continuity of <math>u</math> it follows that the function <math display="block">r\to \int\limits_{\partial B(x, r)}\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!-\, u(y) \,\mathrm{d}S(y)</math> is continuous, and that its [[Limit of a function|limit]] as <math>r\to 0</math> is <math>u(x).</math>
* Spherical means can be used to solve the Cauchy problem for the [[wave equation]]  <math>\partial^2_t u=c^2\,\Delta u</math>  in odd space dimension. The result, known as Kirchhoff's formula, is derived by using spherical means to reduce the wave equation in <math>\R^n</math> (for odd <math>n</math>) to the wave equation in <math>\R</math>, and then using [[d'Alembert's formula]]. The expression itself is presented in [[Wave equation#Scalar wave equation in general dimension and Kirchhoff's formulae|wave equation article]].
* If <math>U</math> is an open set in <math>\mathbb R^n</math> and <math>u</math> is  a [[smooth function|''C''<sup>2</sup>]] function defined on <math>U</math>, then <math>u</math> is [[harmonic function|harmonic]] if and only if for all <math>x</math> in <math>U</math> and all <math>r>0</math> such that the closed ball <math>B(x, r)</math> is contained in <math>U</math> one has <math display="block">u(x)=\int\limits_{\partial B(x, r)}\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!-\, u(y) \, \mathrm{d}S(y).</math> This result can be used to prove the [[maximum principle]] for harmonic functions.
